title: Core Concepts and Conventions
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter introduces the structural foundations of statistical analysis: the distinction between populations and samples, the classification of variables, and the representation of measured characteristics as random variables. It establishes the mathematical language of distributions and conventions used to bridge observed sample data with unknown population properties. ## The Lifecycle of an Empirical Study A scientific investigation proceeds through distinct stages that connect a broader scientific question to concrete empirical data. The primary objective is virtually always to make statements about a broader **population** of interest. However, because of practical, logistical, and financial limitations, it is almost never possible to examine an entire population. Instead, researchers select a subset, termed a **sample**. The methodology governing this process falls into three core branches of statistics: 1. **Study Design (*Proefopzet*):** The researcher specifies the target population, establishes formal protocols for drawing a sample, and defines the full data collection and analysis plan. The design must guarantee that the sample is representative of the population so that valid generalizations can be made. 2. **Data Exploration and Descriptive Statistics (*Data-exploratie en beschrijvende statistiek*):** Once data are collected, they are visualized and summarized. This step yields empirical insight into the data and verifies whether necessary modeling assumptions hold. 3. **Statistical Inference (*Statistische besluitvorming*):** Methods that allow researchers to generalize sample observations to the underlying population, providing formal statements and conclusions at the population level. ### Case Study: The NHANES Dataset To contextualize these principles, we consider data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). Collected periodically since 1960, NHANES records physical, demographic, nutritional, lifestyle, and health indicators across thousands of individuals. For example, a sample of $10\,000$ Americans collected between 2009 and 2012 contains measurements such as: | ID | Gender | Age | Race1 | Weight | Height | BMI | BPSysAve | TotChol | SmokeNow | Smoke100 | |---:|:---|---:|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|:---|:---| | 51624 | male | 34 | White | 87.4 | 164.7 | 32.22 | 113 | 3.49 | No | Yes | | 51625 | male | 4 | Other | 17.0 | 105.4 | 15.30 | NA | NA | NA | NA | | 51630 | female | 49 | White | 86.7 | 168.4 | 30.57 | 112 | 6.70 | Yes | Yes | | 51638 | male | 9 | White | 29.8 | 133.1 | 16.82 | 86 | 4.86 | NA | NA | | 51646 | male | 8 | White | 35.2 | 130.6 | 20.64 | 107 | 4.09 | NA | NA | | 51647 | female | 45 | White | 75.7 | 166.7 | 27.24 | 118 | 5.82 | NA | No | ## Classification of Variables A **variable** is a characteristic that varies from subject to subject (e.g., person to person, animal to animal) in a study. Variables are classified into distinct types: 1. **Qualitative (Categorical) Variables:** Possess non-numerical outcome categories. - **Nominal Variables:** Categories have labels but no intrinsic natural ordering. Examples include gender, biological race, blood type, and eye color. - **Ordinal Variables:** Categories exhibit a natural order, yet the differences between ranks are not quantitatively defined. Examples include World Health Organization (WHO) BMI classifications and smoking status (never smoked, former smoker, active smoker). 2. **Numerical (Quantitative) Variables:** Values correspond to meaningful numerical quantities. - **Discrete Variables:** Result from counting processes. Values take isolated points, typically integers. Examples include the number of lifetime sexual partners, the count of *Plethodon jordani* salamanders in a forest quadrant, or the number of reads mapping to a specific gene in an RNA sequencing experiment. - **Continuous Variables:** Can theoretically take any real value within a given interval. Differences between values can be arbitrarily small. Examples include age, weight, BMI, systolic blood pressure, and fluorescence intensity in an ELISA assay. ### Analytical Nuances in Variable Types * **Dichotomization:** Researchers often convert continuous variables into binary nominal categories (e.g., partitioning systolic blood pressure into normotensive $\leq 140\text{ mm Hg}$ and hypertensive $> 140\text{ mm Hg}$). This practice is generally discouraged because it discards substantial information and makes downstream conclusions sensitive to the choice of cutoff threshold. * **Rounding:** Continuous variables are often rounded when recorded (e.g., age to the nearest integer year, blood pressure to the nearest millimeter of mercury). Despite appearing discrete, they must theoretically be treated as continuous variables. * **Ordinal Coding:** When assigning numerical ranks to ordinal categories (e.g., $1 = \text{never smoked}$, $2 = \text{former smoker}$, $3 = \text{current smoker}$), the arithmetic differences ($3 - 2 = 1$ versus $2 - 1 = 1$) lack metric meaning. One cannot assume that transitioning from non-smoker to former smoker represents the same quantitative shift as transitioning from former smoker to current smoker. ## Target Populations and Inclusion Criteria The ultimate target of an investigation is the **population**. In statistical theory, a population is not merely a static collection of living subjects; it is an abstract concept that includes all current and future entities about which conclusions are sought. Because populations constantly evolve and extend indefinitely into the future, a population is typically modeled as infinitely large and never fully observable. To ensure that an investigation addresses a well-defined cohort, researchers specify rigorous selection criteria: * **Inclusion criteria:** Conditions an experimental unit *must* meet to belong to the study population (e.g., presenting with hypertension, falling within a target age bracket such as 40–65 years, or being of a specific sex). * **Exclusion criteria:** Characteristics that *disqualify* an experimental unit from belonging to the study population (e.g., current medication usage, pregnancy, or co-occurring chronic pathologies). ## Random Variables Before sampling an individual, the exact measurement of a characteristic cannot be known with certainty. To distinguish an unobserved property from an observed measurement: * A **random variable** (denoted by an uppercase letter, $X$) represents the theoretical value of a characteristic obtained through a random draw from the target population prior to measurement. * A **realization** (denoted by a lowercase letter, $x$) is the concrete, observed numerical value obtained after measuring the subject. If a characteristic does not vary across subjects in a population, every draw would yield identical values. Because biological systems exhibit variability, repeated random draws produce differing outcomes. If we plan to measure $n$ independent subjects, their unmeasured states are $n$ random variables, $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$. Once recorded, they produce the realization vector $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$. ## Describing Populations with Probability Distributions The behavior of a continuous random variable $X$ across a population is formalized by its **probability distribution**, characterized by a probability density function (PDF), $f(x)$. The probability that a randomly drawn subject from the population has a value falling within an interval $[a, b]$ corresponds to the area under $f(x)$ over that range: $$ P[a \leq X \leq b] = \int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx $$ Because the variable must fall within the real numbers, the total area under the density function is normalized to 1: $$ P[-\infty < X < \infty] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = 1 $$ The **cumulative distribution function** (CDF), denoted $F(x)$, yields the probability that $X$ takes a value less than or equal to a threshold $x$: $$ F(x) = P[X \leq x] = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(u)\,du $$ Consequently, interval probabilities can be computed directly as differences between CDF evaluations: $$ P[a \leq X \leq b] = F(b) - F(a) $$ ### The Normal Distribution In biological and chemical systems, continuous measurements frequently follow a **Normal distribution**, denoted $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$. The normal distribution is symmetric, bell-shaped, and fully specified by two parameters: its mean $\mu$ and its variance $\sigma^2$ (or standard deviation $\sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}$). Suppose that systolic blood pressure $X$ across healthy adults aged 40–65 is normally distributed with mean $\mu = 120\text{ mm Hg}$ and variance $\sigma^2 = 196\text{ mm Hg}^2$ (standard deviation $\sigma = 14\text{ mm Hg}$). The probability of selecting a random individual with systolic blood pressure between $115$ and $120\text{ mm Hg}$ is: $$ P[115 \leq X \leq 120] = \int_{115}^{120} f(x)\,dx = F(120) - F(115) $$ Using standard computational tools (such as `pnorm()` in R, which takes arguments `mean` and `sd`): $$ F(120) = 0.5, \quad F(115) \approx 0.3605 $$ $$ P[115 \leq X \leq 120] = 0.5 - 0.3605 = 0.1395 \quad (13.95\%) $$ ## Estimating the Population Distribution from a Sample In practice, the true population distribution is unknown and must be estimated from sample realizations $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$. Consider an empirical sample drawn from NHANES by filtering for non-smokers without diabetes, normal BMI, no history of hard drugs, non-poor general health, and absence of sleep trouble, aged 40–65. This selection leaves $n = 275$ individuals with measured systolic blood pressures $x_1, \dots, x_{275}$. ### Non-parametric Histogram Estimation A basic, assumption-free method to approximate the unknown density $f(x)$ is the histogram. Partitioning the measurement space into equal bins of width $h$ (e.g., $h = 5\text{ mm Hg}$), we calculate: 1. **Absolute Frequencies:** The raw count of observations $c_k$ falling in bin $k$. 2. **Relative Frequencies / Densities:** The density height $d_k$ is computed so that the area of the bar corresponds to the probability mass of the bin: $$ d_k = \frac{c_k}{n \cdot h} $$ The probability that an individual has a value in bin $k$ is estimated by: $$ \widehat{P}[X \in \text{bin } k] = d_k \cdot h = \frac{c_k}{n} $$ For the interval $[115, 120\text{ mm Hg})$, the NHANES subset contains 41 individuals out of 275: $$ \widehat{P}[115 \leq X < 120] = \frac{41}{275} \approx 0.1491 \quad (14.91\%) $$ Because all subjects fall into one of the bins, the sum of areas across all histogram bars equals 1: $$ \sum_{k} (d_k \cdot h) = \sum_k \frac{c_k}{n} = 1 $$ ### Parametric Estimation Under Normality When the empirical distribution displays approximate symmetry and a characteristic bell shape, we can adopt a parametric model. Instead of relying solely on local counts within arbitrary bins, we assume $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ and estimate the population parameters using the entire sample: * Sample mean: $\bar{x} = 120.4\text{ mm Hg}$ * Sample standard deviation: $s = \sqrt{129.8} \approx 11.39\text{ mm Hg}$ Plugging these estimates directly into the normal cumulative distribution function yields: $$ \widehat{P}[115 \leq X \leq 120] = \Phi\left(\frac{120 - 120.4}{11.39}\right) - \Phi\left(\frac{115 - 120.4}{11.39}\right) \approx 0.1397 \quad (13.97\%) $$ Parametric estimation is generally more efficient and precise than bin counts because all $n$ data points contribute to identifying $\bar{x}$ and $s$. However, this gain in precision relies strictly on the validity of the distributional assumption. Assessing whether such assumptions are reasonable is a primary objective of exploratory data analysis. ### Defining Extreme Thresholds Distributional estimates allow researchers to determine reference intervals and clinical cutoffs. For example, to identify a blood pressure threshold $t_{\text{threshold}}$ that is exceeded by only $5\%$ of healthy individuals: $$ P(X > t_{\text{threshold}}) = 0.05 \iff P(X \leq t_{\text{threshold}}) = 0.95 $$ Evaluating the 95th quantile of the estimated normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(120.4, 11.39^2)$: $$ t_{\text{threshold}} = \bar{x} + z_{0.95} \cdot s \approx 120.4 + (1.645 \cdot 11.39) \approx 142.6\text{ mm Hg} $$ This derived threshold aligns closely with the conventional clinical benchmark of $140\text{ mm Hg}$ used to diagnose hypertension. ## Statistics Versus Parameters A central structural convention in statistics is the distinction between population quantities and sample quantities: * **Parameters:** Fixed, typically unknown constants that describe the true population distribution. By standard convention, parameters are denoted by Greek letters (e.g., $\mu, \sigma^2$). * **Statistics:** Quantities calculated directly from observed sample data. Because a statistic depends on the specific sample drawn, its value varies from sample to sample. Prior to sample collection, a statistic is a random variable and is written with an uppercase letter (e.g., $\bar{X}$). Once calculated on an observed sample, its realized numerical value is written with a lowercase letter (e.g., $\bar{x}$). | Population Parameter (Fixed, Unobserved) | Sample Statistic (Estimator, Random Variable) | Realized Value (Observed Number) | |:---:|:---:|:---:| | Mean: $\mu$ | $\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ | $\bar{x}$ | | Variance: $\sigma^2$ | $S^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2$ | $s^2$ | Sample statistics serve as estimators of population parameters. Quantifying the error and variability of these estimators under repeated sampling is the domain of statistical inference. ## Sources * **Chapter 2 Introduction & Section 2.1:** Scientific study steps, branches of statistics, definition and classification of variables (nominal, ordinal, discrete, continuous), dichotomy pitfalls, and the NHANES introductory dataset. * **Section 2.2:** Target population definition, temporal open-endedness, inclusion and exclusion criteria. * **Section 2.3 & 2.5:** Random variables ($X$ vs $x$), stochastic sampling variability, and sample selection of healthy NHANES subjects ($n = 275$). * **Section 2.4 & 2.6:** Probability distributions, PDFs, CDFs, normal model calculations, non-parametric histogram estimation, parametric density estimation, and clinical threshold determination. * **Section 2.7:** Formal distinction and notation conventions between population parameters and sample statistics.
